title: The Myth of Copying Things Down
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton opens with a book scrutiny in which a senior leader criticised a teacher's sparse exercise books despite her students' strong results, and uses it to challenge what he calls the Myth of Copying Things Down: the belief that copying something makes it make sense and that copying it ensures it will be remembered. He argues neither holds, and that accountability systems reward full books as proxies for effort, understanding and retention when they are poor proxies. His stronger claim is that copying can harm learning, both by consuming lesson time and by removing any incentive to think, since a book that looks like thinking lets students avoid thinking. He offers four remedies of escalating boldness: separate listening from copying, make copying active, move copying later in the lesson when material makes sense, or drop classroom copying altogether. The most important alternative is to spend the saved time checking understanding, for example with mini-whiteboard 'your turn' examples after a model. The piece closes by inviting maths teachers to weigh whether full books are the learning proxy they hope for, and includes reader responses including a dissenting case for copying structure.
points: Barton's hypothesis is that students fail to understand what they copy because copying removes the incentive to think: a book that looks like thinking lets them avoid doing any.
He criticises book-scrutiny culture for treating copied objectives, notes, worked examples and purple-pen corrections as proxies for effort and retention.
Copying while the teacher explains creates split attention, so he argues that listening and watching should be separated from writing.

His preferred alternative replaces copying a worked example with an immediate similar problem on mini-whiteboards, giving the teacher mass-participation evidence of understanding in about the same time.
quotes: Nothing magical happens in the process of transferring something that makes little or no sense from the board to a book. And if it does not make sense now, it feels like a pretty big gamble to hope it will make sense and stick in the future.
More specifically, books filled with lesson objectives, notes, worked examples, and corrections are regarded as proxies for effort, understanding, and retention. But I think they are poor proxies.

The way worked examples and corrections play out in many classrooms is the teacher explains and the students sit there patiently waiting for the teacher to finish. An unlucky few might be asked a question, but most can zone out until they are asked to pick up their pens and copy whatever is on the board into their books. The fact that students end up with something in their book that looks like thinking is the very reason they can get away without doing any thinking.

Or students are wrestling to deal with the split attention caused by processing the words they are hearing with the notes they are reading and writing. I am convinced that the actions of listening and watching should be separated from the act of copying.

And students only really know if they have understood a correction once they have tried a similar question to the one they got wrong. Shifting the time we ask students to copy down lesson objectives, notes, worked examples and corrections to later in the lesson will allow students to attach more meaning to them.

And remember, copying each of these things down has a cost, both in the lesson time they take and the way they reduce the need to think. Here is a key question to ask yourself: if your students did not have to copy down lesson objectives, worked examples, and corrections, how else could you use that time?

I also have no idea if this is true in subjects other than maths. I just want you to consider whether books full of such things really are the proxy for learning we hope they are, and if there is anything better we could do with our classroom time.
